title: What the Studio is
body: # Overview

The Studio is where you build a world setup: a folder of files that tells Worldgen V2 how to generate a world. You edit it with forms and node graphs, and see the result on a map or in the world you are standing in.
# The pieces
- World Settings: the height of the world and sea level.
- Dimensions: the overworld and any other dimension. Each one says which biomes exist, where, and what else is generated.
- Biomes: what the ground is made of and what grows on it. A biome is a small graph of nodes.
- Zones, Placement rules and Prefabs are optional extras.
# Opening it
Press G, type /studio, or press the Studio button on the pause screen. Inside a world it opens the setup that world was made from.

title: World setups and worlds
body: # A world remembers its setup

When you create a world you choose a world setup on the Customize screen. The world keeps that setup for good (it is saved in the world's folder), so choosing a different setup for the next world never changes the old one.
# Editing a world
Opening the Studio in a world edits that world's setup. Press Apply to recompile it into the world. New chunks use the change at once; use Regen to rebuild chunks that already exist.
# Heights
World Settings sets Min Y and the depth. A world gets the height its setup asks for when it is created. The default is Y -64 to 320. Existing worlds keep their height.

title: The top bar
body: # Buttons
- Undo and Redo go through every edit in this setup.
- Save writes your changes to disk (Ctrl+S).
- Apply saves and recompiles the setup into the world you are in (Ctrl+Enter).
- Regen rebuilds every chunk generated so far, so old terrain picks up the change. Blocks you placed in those chunks are replaced.
- Live rebuilds only a square of chunks around you after each edit, so you watch your change happen. Pin moves the square to where you stand, and the r button sets how big it is.
- Guide opens this guide.

title: The dimension editor
body: # Biomes come from
Choose Your biome pool for random regions of the biomes you list, or a Hytale zone to let Hytale's own map decide where its biomes go. While a Hytale zone is chosen your pool is not used.
# Biome pool

Each row is a biome the dimension may use. Weight is how common it is compared with the others. Size makes its regions bigger or smaller. Blend is how far it fades into its neighbours. Add all missing adds every biome you have made.
# Features

Zones, spawn structure, connected structures, points of interest, placement rules, ores, terrain shapes and pillar rings each have Off, Default and Custom. Off does nothing (your settings are kept). Default is the built-in behaviour. Custom is yours to edit.
# World edge, rivers, caves, oceans

Base block and Fluid are the stone and liquid the world is made of. Rivers and caves can be classic (simple settings) or a node graph in the Hytale way. Ocean depth scales how deep the seas are without touching land.
# The map
The Map shows the biome layout from the real engine. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom. Click a spot to teleport there while in a world.

title: The biome editor
body: # Form view

Name, category and the Minecraft biome it uses for sky colour, grass colour, mobs and music. Weight, size and blend decide how often and how large it appears. The climate pad places it among its neighbours.
# Graph view

The graph is the biome. Its output node has three sockets: Terrain (a density that shapes the ground), Material (what the ground is made of) and Props (what grows or is built on it). Wire nodes into those sockets.
# JSON view
Shows the same biome as text. Everything the graph can do is here too, and you can paste in nodes from Hytale files.

title: Using the node graph
body: # Adding nodes
Double-click a node or empty space, or right-click, to open a search box. Type part of a name and press Enter. Or click an empty input on a node to add something that fits it.
# Moving around
Drag empty space to pan and scroll to zoom. Press F to fit everything on screen.
# Editing
Click a node to see its settings on the right. Right-click for Wrap in, Replace with, Duplicate, Copy and Delete. Delete or Backspace removes the selected node and what is under it.
# Blocks
Any block field has a Pick button: a searchable list of every block with its picture.

title: How terrain is made
body: # Density
Terrain is a number for every point in space. Above zero the point is solid, below zero it is air. The surface is where the number crosses zero.
# Building a hill

Start with a vertical gradient (high near the ground, falling with height), add a noise so it varies from place to place, and the zero line becomes rolling ground. Add more noise at a larger scale for mountains. Multiply a noise by another to make some areas flat and others rough.
# Why nodes
Each node does one small job: make noise, add two things, clamp, remap with a curve. Wiring them together builds the field.

title: Materials and props
body: # Materials

A material provider says what block goes at each spot of solid ground: for example grass on top, then dirt, then stone. Queue tries its children in order, SpaceAndDepth measures how deep a block is below the surface, and Constant is one block everywhere.
# Props

A prop is something placed on the ground: a tree, a bush, a rock, a prefab. Positions decide where to try, a scanner searches for a good spot, and the prop is built there. Masks stop props replacing or covering the wrong blocks.

title: Using Hytale's content
body: # Hytale assets

If Hytale is installed, a dimension can read its files in place. Set hytale.assets to the Assets.zip path and hytale.worldStructure to a zone such as Zone1_Plains1. Nothing is copied; it is read when the setup compiles.
# Importing a biome
The plus next to Biomes offers every Hytale biome. Importing copies it into your setup so you can edit it.
# Blocks
Hytale block names are mapped to the nearest Minecraft block. Stairs, halves, logs, vines and dripstone keep their orientation.

title: The kinds of node
body: # Why there are kinds
Every node has a kind, shown by its colour, and a socket only accepts nodes of the right kind. This is what stops you plugging a block into a noise.
# The kinds
- Density (green): a number for every point in space. Terrain is a density. Above zero is solid, below is air.
- Curve (blue): a function of one number, drawn as a line. Used to reshape values, for example to make hills steeper near the top.
- Vector (orange): a direction or position in space, used to warp or push a density around.
- Material (purple): decides which block goes at a spot of solid ground.
- Pattern (pink): a yes or no question about the blocks around a spot, such as 'is this the surface' or 'is the ground flat enough'.
- Positions (teal): a set of points, such as one per tree or one per boulder.
- Scanner (light blue): a way of searching around a point for a good spot to build.
- Assignments (yellow): says which prop goes at which position, often with weights.
- Prop (gold): something to build: a block, a box of blocks, a prefab, a whole tree.
- Mask: blocks a prop may not be placed over or may not replace.
# Reading a socket
A node's inputs are listed on the left of the node, and its output is the dot on the right. Drag from an output to an input of the same colour to connect them.

title: Words used in the Studio
body: # Glossary
- World setup: a folder of files that describes how to generate a world. Each world remembers the one it was made from.
- Dimension: one world such as the overworld. It lists which biomes it uses and what else to generate.
- Biome: terrain, materials and props for one kind of place.
- Zone: a large region of the world that uses its own set of biomes.
- Prefab: a saved structure of blocks that can be placed in the world.
- Prop: anything placed on the ground by a biome.
- Density: a number at every point in space. Above zero is solid, below zero is air.
- Octave: one layer of a noise. More octaves add finer detail.
- Frequency and scale: frequency is how many times a noise repeats per block. Scale is the opposite, the width in blocks of one repeat.
- Seed: a number that picks one particular random pattern. The same seed always gives the same world.
- Apply: save the setup and recompile it into the world you are in.
- Regen: rebuild chunks that already exist so they use the current setup.

title: The map and live preview
body: # The map

In the dimension editor the Map shows the biome layout the real engine would give. Zones tints the regions, Slice shows a vertical cut, Spawn and Fit recentre. Hover a spot to see its coordinates and biome.
# Seeing a change in the world

Edit, press Apply, then Regen to rebuild what is already generated. Faster: turn Live on. The chunks around you rebuild a moment after each edit, so you see the change as you make it. Pin moves the live square to where you stand and the r button changes how big it is.
# Tip
Fly up and look straight down while Live is on. Changing a noise setting reshapes the ground in front of you.

title: Spawn, landmarks, rivers, caves and ores
body: # Spawn structure
A prefab placed where players start. You choose the prefab, where it goes, its rotation, how deep it is buried, and an optional crater around it.
# Connected structures and points of interest

Landmarks are placed relative to each other (a village, with a ruin to the north). A road can join a landmark to its parent. Points of interest scatter a fixed number of structures between two distances.
# Placement rules
A rule looks for a place (a finder), checks conditions (the biome, the slope, water nearby) and builds something (an action). They are built as nodes. The fallen tree across a river is one.
# Rivers and caves
Each can be classic, with simple settings such as width and depth, or a node graph in Hytale's way. Rivers follow the land, so the water sits level with it.
# Ores
Each ore rule says which block, how big a vein, how many veins, and between which heights. Nothing from vanilla generates, so all ore comes from these.

title: World height and sea level
body: # Where it is set
World Settings has Min Y, World depth and Sea level. Ceiling is Min Y plus depth.
# Presets
Standard is Y -64 to 320. There are Hytale presets (0 to 320, 0 to 512, -64 to 512) and a very tall one. Choose Custom to set your own. Use multiples of 16.
# When it applies

A world gets the height its setup asks for when it is created. Save the setup, then create the world. A height you have not used before is ready the next time the Create World screen opens. Vanilla shows a one-time experimental warning for such worlds.

title: My biomes do not show up
body: # Check the biome map
In the dimension editor, look at Biomes come from. If a Hytale zone is chosen, Hytale's own map decides the biomes and your pool is ignored. Switch it to Your biome pool.
# Check the pool
A biome must be in the pool and enabled (the tick on its row). Weight 0 means never.
# Rebuild what exists
Chunks already generated keep their old biome. Press Apply and then Regen, or use Live.

title: The ground is flat, empty or all stone
body: # Flat ground
A terrain with only a vertical gradient is a flat sheet. Add a noise and add it to the gradient (a SumDensity) to get hills.
# Nothing generates

The terrain must be positive (solid) somewhere and negative (air) somewhere. A density that is always positive fills the whole world, one that is always negative is empty. Try the demo on the node's page to see what it does alone.
# All stone

The materials decide the blocks. A Queue tries its rules in order and falls back to its fallback, which is stone by default. Check that your surface rule's pattern really matches (surface, flat enough, enough air above).
# Weird sheer walls
Large noise amplitude against a small gradient scale makes cliffs. Lower the amplitude or raise the scale.

title: Changes do not appear in the world
body: # Apply, then Regen
Edits happen in the Studio. Apply recompiles them into the world, and new chunks use them. Existing chunks need Regen.
# Which setup is the world using?
The top bar says whether you are editing this world's setup. If it says the world uses another one, Apply will switch the world to the one you have open.
# Saving
Apply saves first. Closing the Studio without saving keeps your edits in memory only until you close the game.

title: Keyboard shortcuts
body: # Everywhere
- G or /studio: open or close the Studio.
- Ctrl+S: save. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y: undo and redo.
- Ctrl+Enter: Apply. Ctrl+J: show or hide the problems list.
# In the graph
- Double-click or right-click: add a node.
- Delete or Backspace: remove the selected node and what is under it.
- F: fit everything on screen.
- Scroll: zoom. Drag empty space: pan.
